En septembre 2026, l'inflation accélère,: In September 2026, inflation picked up, driven by energy. In the United States, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 3.6% year on year, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis (29 October). In the euro area, the harmonised index rose 3.8%, with energy up 18.9%, according to Eurostat (16 October). In Japan, the national index rose 2.1%, according to the Statistics Bureau (23 October). All three central banks aim for 2%. But that figure does not mean the same thing at the Fed, the ECB and the Bank of Japan (BoJ): coverage, the weight of housing and formulas differ. This article explains how to read these indices, where inflation comes from, why it persists and why Japan faces the opposite problem.
Le 28 octobre 2026, la gouverneure Lisa: On 28 October 2026, Governor Lisa Cook voted for a rate hike that the majority of the Federal Reserve's monetary policy committee rejected. On 29 June, the Supreme Court had rejected, by five votes to four, the government's application in the case arising from the attempt to remove her. Kevin Warsh has chaired the Fed since 22 May; on 29 October the European Central Bank announced Christine Lagarde's early departure. These facts say nothing about anyone's intentions. They raise a question: what grounds a central bank's independence, what protects it, and how can it wear down? The article goes back over the theoretical argument, compares the three legal frameworks and separates what 2026 establishes from what remains to be confirmed.
Entre le 10 et le 18 septembre 2026, la: Between 10 and 18 September 2026, the ECB, the Fed and the Bank of Japan (BoJ) raised their policy rates by 25 basis points (bp), or 0.25 percentage point, before holding them at the end of October. Money market rates followed within days; household credit runs on a different clock: in the week of 1 October, a 30-year fixed-rate US mortgage cost 7.28%, against 6.34% a year earlier, tracking the 10-year yield more than the policy rate. What does a 25 bp hike change, and what can it do against energy-driven inflation? The article follows the chain down to credit, separating what is observed from what is estimated.
Le 14 octobre 2026, la presse citait, d': On 14 October 2026, the press cited, based on the Chicago exchange's (CME) FedWatch tool, a 41.5% probability that the Federal Reserve (Fed) would raise its rates on 28 October. On the morning of the 28th, the same tool, cited by another source, showed only 7.2%. The Fed held its rates, with two votes for a hike, and a December hike was still priced at about 83% after the press conference. So what did “the market” expect? The phrase means nothing without a date, an instrument and assumptions. This article shows how a price becomes a probability, what the calculation assumes, why European and Japanese figures vary by source, and what separates a price from a survey or a projection, for rates as for inflation.
Le 5 octobre 2026, le rendement de l'emp: On 5 October 2026, the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note reached 5.31% in the San Francisco Fed's data, 107 basis points (bp), or 1.07 percentage points, more than a year earlier. Two explanations compete: the market expects higher short-term rates, or it demands a larger premium for lending long. This split cannot be observed. It comes out of a model, and two Fed models do not estimate the same premium. This article describes the moves in the US yield curve since the end of 2025, shows what the published decomposition allows us to say, examines the role of central bank balance sheets, and recalls what Japan learned when its central bank set the long-term rate itself.
